prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I hold two fingers to my head, trigger my thumb, I say pow. I slice my throat with a single stroke, pull an invisible blade vertically along my vein. Remember the deaths we did together? Twiddling oven knobs in the air then thrusting our chins to inhale? I loved you so much during that experimental play when you slowly leant forward to nick your femoral artery then quietly bled out in your seat until curtain call, blood only we saw. As well as death, we’d mime marriage. I’d slide on a spectral ring and you’d shiver at the thrill of my thumb and fingertip sealing the deal for a second till the thought melted back into your skin. I am proficient at beginnings, the Air Year: the anniversary prior to paper for which ephemeral gifts are traditional. Only after our rings became solid silver did they truly disappear. Now the house is a mime scene. Mime blood all over the floor, trodden into carpet fibers, shirts, bras, dried to an airy crust under my nails. I slit my neck at the traffic lights, pow on the train, I suspend my non-knife above my head, “see what you’re making me do.” Red whirls rise from the cuts. All these huge thoughts come to nothing. My shadow is the chalk outline of a woman who did not jump.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Remember, Twiddling, Air

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text, refined for rhythm and precision while preserving its imagery and meaning:

---

I press two fingers to my temple, cock my thumb, and whisper *pow*. I draw an invisible blade in one clean stroke across my throat, tracing the line of my vein. Do you remember the deaths we performed together? Turning phantom oven knobs in the air, then tilting our chins back to breathe them in? I loved you most during that experimental piece, when you leaned slowly forward to nick your femoral artery and bled out quietly in your seat until curtain call—blood that only we could see. Alongside death, we rehearsed marriage too. I would slide a spectral ring onto your finger, and you'd shiver as my thumb and fingertip sealed the vow for a fleeting second before the sensation dissolved back into your skin. I have always excelled at beginnings—the Air Year, that anniversary preceding paper, when gifts are meant to be weightless and fleeting. It was only once our rings turned to solid silver that they truly vanished.

Now the house has become a mime's stage. Phantom blood stains everything—ground into the carpet fibers, soaked into shirts and bras, dried to a papery crust beneath my fingernails. I slit my throat at the traffic lights, mime a gunshot on the train, hold my invisible blade aloft: *see what you're making me do.* Red spirals rise from wounds that aren't there. All these enormous thoughts amount to nothing. My shadow is the chalk outline of a woman who never jumped.
outputs.L2:
I press two fingers against my temple, cock my thumb back, whisper "bang." With one smooth gesture I draw a phantom blade straight up the length of my throat, tracing the vein. Do you recall those imagined deaths we performed together? Cranking phantom gas dials through empty air before bowing our heads to breathe it in? I adored you completely during that improvised scene where you tilted forward gradually, nicked the artery in your thigh, and bled silently in your chair until the final curtain—a wound visible only to us.

Beyond death, we also acted out weddings. I'd slip a nonexistent ring onto your finger, and you'd tremble as my thumb and forefinger pressed together in a fleeting ceremony, the sensation dissolving back into your flesh moments later. I excel at the early stages of things—what I call the Air Year, that anniversary occurring before the paper one, marked traditionally by gifts as insubstantial as breath. It wasn't until our rings solidified into actual silver that they genuinely vanished from our lives.

The house has become a stage for pantomime now. Imaginary blood coats everything—ground into the carpet fibers, staining shirts and undergarments, hardening into a weightless residue beneath my fingernails. I draw my finger across my throat while waiting at intersections, mouth "bang" on the train, hold my invisible weapon above my skull—"look at what you're forcing me to do." Crimson spirals seem to lift from the invisible wounds.

All these massive, weighty thoughts amount to nothing in the end. What remains of me is merely the chalk silhouette of a woman who never actually leapt.
outputs.L3:
We used to play at dying together, my partner and I—turning our bodies into weapons and wounds in the same breath. I would mime a knife into his ribs; he'd stagger back, clutch his chest, mouth open in silent theater, and collapse into laughter or into my arms, whichever came first. It was our private language, absurd and tender, a way of holding mortality at arm's length by making it small enough to hold in our hands. We died for each other constantly, and each death was a kind of intimacy—proof that we trusted one another enough to fall, again and again, into pretend oblivion.

Marriage, too, became part of the game. We had no rings of gold or silver, only air—an invisible band I'd slide onto his finger, or he onto mine, sealing vows we invented on the spot. For a moment, something would flicker between us, some fragile current of meaning, as if the gesture alone could conjure a future. Then it would dissolve, the way breath fogs a window and disappears. We called it our Air Year, half-joking, half-serious, borrowing the language of anniversaries—paper, cotton, silver—but ours was made of nothing, weightless, and somehow that nothingness felt more honest than any object could.

Looking back, I understand now that the meaning lived precisely in that impermanence. The invisible ring meant something because it asked nothing of us—it existed only in the moment we chose to believe in it, then vanished, leaving no residue of obligation. But when things shifted, when the symbolic became literal—when air was meant to harden into solid silver, into something worn daily, weighed, appraised—the meaning didn't deepen. It collapsed. What had been sacred in its lightness became unbearable in its permanence. The moment we tried to make it real, it stopped being ours.

Since we ended, I haven't stopped playing dead. It's become involuntary, almost liturgical—waiting for a bus, standing in a checkout line, walking through a crowded street, I'll feel my hand curl into the shape of a gun, or my fingers trace an invisible blade across my throat. No one around me knows what it means. To them, it's a stranger's odd tic, a private twitch. But for me, it's a ritual of grief, a way of metabolizing an absence too large to speak aloud. Each mimed death is a small confession, a way of saying: this is what it feels like, this is how much it hurt, without ever having to say the words.

Beneath these gestures, though, something darker moves—an undertow I try not to name. The playful deaths of our shared past have curdled into something more solitary, more dangerous. Sometimes I catch myself standing near a ledge, or watching traffic a beat too long, and I wonder if the games we once played were rehearsals for something my mind refuses to fully admit. I think of a woman I once saw—or imagined—on a rooftop, her shadow stretched long against the wall, poised at the edge but never leaping. She didn't jump. But her shadow lingers in me still, a haunting outline of what almost was, a silhouette of grief that never resolved into resolution, only into the quiet, persistent shape of survival.
outputs.L4:
# On Mimed Violence and Ephemeral Vows

Throughout this exploration of intimacy, the poet returns again and again to a peculiar choreography: gestures of death performed in play, gestures of marriage performed in earnest, both existing in the same charged space between two people who have built their partnership on ritual repetition. A hand raised as if to strike, then withdrawn. A finger circled as if placing a ring, then released into air. These motions accumulate meaning through their very falseness—the violence that never lands, the commitment that exists only in the moment of gesture.

The invisible violence functions as a kind of testing ground. When one partner mimes a blow that stops short of contact, or traces the outline of a wound that never bleeds, something essential about vulnerability and trust gets rehearsed without the danger of actual harm. This is intimacy as theater, but theater with real stakes—each performance of near-violence asks a question: *do you trust me enough to stop? do I trust you enough to let you come this close?* The poem suggests that such enacted danger, precisely because it remains imaginary, can hold and examine fears that would be unbearable if spoken directly.

Parallel to this runs the motif of the ephemeral wedding ring—rings made of grass, of breath, of gesture alone, circling fingers and vanishing. These temporary bindings echo the invisible violence in their insubstantiality; both are acts of profound significance that leave no mark, no evidence, nothing but the memory of the gesture itself. The wedding ring that isn't really there becomes a way of solemnizing the relationship again and again, a renewable vow that costs nothing and risks nothing—until, the poem suggests, it does.

The turn comes when these imagined gestures calcify into the literal: actual silver rings, actual metal weight on the finger, permanence made material. One might expect this transition—from ephemeral to eternal, from mimed to real—to bring relief, to fix the relationship into something stable and safe. Instead, the poem reveals a devastating irony: once the rings become real, the imagined violence that had always existed alongside them becomes real too, or at least realer, more threatening. The invisible gesture, once harmless because it was understood as pure performance, now carries the weight of what permanent commitment actually risks. If the marriage is real, then perhaps the violence was never entirely imaginary either.

This paradox culminates in an image that refuses resolution: violence suspended mid-gesture, forever about to happen but never completing itself. The poem ends not in catastrophe but in the unbearable tension of catastrophe's possibility—a moment stretched taut between danger and safety, harm and its absence. This is despair without event, threat without action, a marriage that has become both more real and more precarious in the same instant. The reader is left holding this suspended moment, understanding that the greatest violence in the poem may be this very suspension: the permanent uncertainty of a gesture that could, at any moment, become real.
outputs.L5:
# Remember

I remember the summer afternoons best—the ones where time seemed to thicken like honey, and there was nothing to do but wait. My grandfather would sit on the porch, twiddling his thumbs in slow, hypnotic circles, a habit he'd picked up from decades of waiting rooms and long car rides. I used to think it was strange, this small, repetitive motion that seemed to soothe something restless in him.

"What are you thinking about?" I'd ask.

"Nothing," he'd say. "Just passing the air through my hands."

I didn't understand what he meant then. Now I do.

There's a particular kind of stillness that comes from twiddling—your hands occupied, your mind free to wander through memory's corridors. It's almost meditative, this small fidgeting, a physical anchor while the mind drifts elsewhere. My grandfather's hands moved, but his thoughts traveled: back to his childhood, to friends long gone, to the woman he'd loved and lost and found again.

The air around us on those porch evenings held everything unspoken. It carried the scent of cut grass, distant rain, his pipe tobacco. Air is strange that way—invisible, essential, and yet we rarely think about it until it's disturbed, until a breeze shifts or a held breath finally releases.

I think about him now, twiddling his thumbs on some porch of memory, and I find myself doing the same thing when I'm anxious or thoughtful. My fingers circle each other, a silent rhythm, and I remember him—not through grand gestures or profound words, but through this small, inherited habit. The air I breathe now is the same air, in some cosmic recycling, that once passed through his lungs, his hands, his quiet afternoons.

Memory works like that: it's not always the air is thin between where we are and where we've been. Sometimes it takes something as simple as twiddling thumbs to remember someone whole.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about a couple who mime acts of violence and love as a metaphor for a decaying marriage.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Theater of Hands

They perform breakfast like a war reenactment. He mimes the pouring of coffee that isn't there, tilting an invisible pot toward a cup that has been empty since the Eisenhower administration. She applauds with her eyes only, the rest of her body still negotiating a ceasefire with the bedsheets.

This is how they've learned to love each other: at a distance, in gesture, with the sound turned off.

His hand becomes a gun some mornings. Fingers cocked, thumb the hammer, and he shoots her across the kitchen table without malice, just habit, the way other men check their phones. She clutches her chest and dies beautifully, has died beautifully for eleven years, has gotten so good at dying that sometimes she forgets to come back to life until noon.

*Bang*, he doesn't say. He doesn't need to. The silence has learned the choreography.

In the evenings, they mime tenderness instead. He cups her face in hands that don't quite touch her face—there's a marriage-length inch between his palm and her cheek, a canyon carved by years of almost. She leans into the absence anyway. It's warmer there than she expected. All the warmth they used to keep in words now lives in the space between gestures, homeless, waiting.

The neighbors think they're strange, these two adults performing charades in their bay window every night, but no one has ever guessed the game. *Sounds like: shattered. Sounds like: sorry. Sounds like: stay.*

She mimes crying sometimes, just to see if he remembers what it looks like. He does. He always does. He's a scholar of her sadness, has memorized its topology, could draw you a map of every place grief pools in her face like rainwater in a pothole. This, too, is love, isn't it? To know the shape of someone's ruin so intimately you could rebuild it in the dark.

At night, they mime the act itself—the one that made them a couple, once, in some ancient geological era of their bodies. He moves above her like weather that's already passed. She receives him like a country that's stopped being surprised by drought. Their hips speak a language that used to have vowels. Now it's all consonants, hard stops, punctuation without sentences.

Afterward, they lie in the dark and mime sleep, each performing unconsciousness for the other's benefit, two actors who've forgotten they're allowed to leave the stage.

Somewhere in the third act of this marriage, they stopped noticing the fourth wall was never there. The audience—if there ever was one—left decades ago. But you don't stop a performance just because the seats are empty. You don't stop mining tenderness from a quarry that's already collapsed.

He shoots her again this morning, over toast.

She dies again, right on cue.

They've gotten so good at their parts they've forgotten there might be other scripts, other rooms, other hands that could hold without almost, without echo, without the terrible grace of gestures that mean everything because they've stopped meaning anything at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of literary fiction using the recurring motif of "mime" gestures—like shooting, slitting throats, and putting on rings—to explore emotional abuse in a relationship.
counterfactuals.output:
# Charades

He proposed with his hands empty. We were at the bar where we'd had our first date, and halfway through his second beer he set it down, looked at me with a seriousness that made my stomach drop, and mimed slipping a ring onto my finger—slow, deliberate, his thumb pressing an invisible band into place. Then he smiled like it was nothing. "When I have the money," he said. "But you get the idea."

I told everyone that story for years. I thought it was romantic, the specificity of it. He was a person who communicated in gesture before he trusted himself with words, and I found that endearing, the way you find a stutter endearing in someone you love, evidence of some deeper feeling straining against the plumbing of speech.

It became our language. In restaurants, when a waiter hovered too long, he'd catch my eye and mime a small, courteous throat-slit—*get rid of them*—and I'd laugh into my napkin. When his mother called at a bad time he'd hold up the phone, point the screen at me, and shoot me with his thumb and forefinger, eyes rolling, *this is going to kill me*. I collected these gestures like inside jokes, which is what they were, at first. A whole grammar built for two people who thought they'd never run out of things to say to each other and so could afford to say some of them silently.

I want to be precise about when it changed, but precision is the first casualty. There wasn't a night. There was a slow substitution, the way a word repeated too many times stops meaning anything and then means something else entirely.

It was maybe eight months in. I'd made a joke at dinner with his friends—nothing, a small thing, a callback to something he'd said the week before that hadn't landed the way I meant it to. He laughed along with the table. Later, in the car, he was quiet in a way I was learning to read as weather. At the red light he turned to me, unsmiling, and put the gun to his own temple. Pulled the trigger. Let his head loll.

"What was that," I said, though I understood it perfectly. It meant: *you embarrassed me. I would rather die than be embarrassed by you again.*

"Nothing," he said. "Just being dumb."

But he didn't speak to me for the rest of the drive, and I spent it working backward through the dinner, cataloguing every sentence I'd said, until I arrived at the joke and turned it over and over like a stone I was trying to find the sharp edge of. By the time we got home I had apologized three times for something neither of us had named.

That was the trick of it, I understand now. The gestures let him say the cruelest things without ever having said them. If I brought it up—*why did you do that in the car*—he could say *do what*, all wounded innocence, and I would be the one who'd turned a joke into an accusation, who couldn't take a joke, who was, as he sometimes said with real tenderness in his voice, *too much*. The gestures were deniable. They left no fingerprints. He could shoot himself in the head at a red light and an hour later hold my face in both hands and tell me I was the only good thing that had ever happened to him, and both of those could be true, and I was the one required to hold them together, to be the place where the contradiction didn't tear.

The throat-slit came out more often after that. Not always for other people. Sometimes for me, quick and small, when I was mid-sentence in front of people we knew—a joke, ostensibly, *cut, that's enough*, and the room would laugh because it was funny, the visual of it, his hand flat and swift against his own neck, and I would laugh too because what else do you do, and I would stop talking. I got very good at stopping. I want to tell you I noticed myself doing it and minded, but for a long time I experienced it the way you experience the outline of a bruise before you understand you've been hit—as pressure, as a vague ache whose origin you can't quite locate, easier to attribute to something you did than something being done to you.

The ring came back into rotation too, which is the part I still turn over most, the part that resists the shape I want to give it. After a fight—and by then we had real fights, the kind with slammed cupboards and my name said like a verdict—he would find me wherever I'd retreated to and, without a word, mime it again: the invisible band, slow, onto my finger. As if the gesture were a apology and a promise fused into one, as if love were a thing you could reissue like a check that had bounced. And it worked on me every time, some animal part of me responding to the old gesture the way you'd respond to a bell that used to mean food. I would feel the fight drain out of my body. I would let him pull me in.

Here is what I did not let myself think for a long time: that all three gestures were the same gesture. That the ring and the gun and the blade at the throat were three faces of a single hand, and the hand was saying, in every version, *I am the one who decides.* I decide when we're joking. I decide when you've gone too far. I decide when it's over and I decide when we begin again, and I will never have to say any of it in words you could quote back to me later, in a kitchen, with a friend, with a lawyer, with yourself at three in the morning trying to explain to the ceiling why you feel the way you feel about a person who has never once, you'll insist, raised a hand to you.

He never did. I want that on the record, for whatever it's worth, which I've come to believe is less than people think. He never touched me. He mimed touching me, and there is, it turns out, an entire architecture you can build out of the difference between a thing and its gesture, a house you can live in for years without noticing it has no doors, only the shapes of doors, painted on, convincing from a distance.

The last time, we were on the porch. It was late spring, the kind of evening that makes you forgive a place for its whole winter. I had said something true—I don't remember what, only that it was true, and small, and not aimed at him at all—and he went very still and then, without looking at me, drew his finger across his throat. Slow. Almost gentle. As if he were sorry to have to do it.

And I felt the old response start up in my chest, the apology already assembling itself behind my teeth, and then—I can't explain this part except to say that some doors, painted on for years, will occasionally, under the right light, reveal themselves as painted—I felt something else instead. I looked at his hand, at the small competent violence of it, at how practiced it was, how it required no thought at all anymore, muscle memory standing in for feeling the way it had for months, maybe years.

"Say it," I said.

He looked at me.

"Whatever that means. Say it with your mouth."

He didn't, of course. That was rather the point of him, and I understood, watching his hand fall back into his lap, empty and suddenly just a hand again, five ordinary fingers with nothing in them, that he might not, in fact, know how. That the gestures weren't a shorthand for something he could also say in full. They might have been the whole vocabulary. Every fluent cruelty he had, translated out of language entirely so that neither of us would ever have to hear it spoken aloud, so that it could go on forever in that gray country where nothing is ever quite said and so nothing can ever quite be answered for.

I put my hand up between us, not quite touching him, and mimed nothing at all. Just held it there, open, empty, until he looked away first.

I moved out six weeks later. He helped carry boxes to the car, and when we were done he stood in the driveway and, out of pure habit, or grief, or the last thing his hands knew how to say, lifted an invisible ring and slid it slowly onto his own finger this time, not mine, and I have thought about that more than almost anything else from those years—what he meant by turning it on himself, whether it was an apology or an accusation or simply the only sentence he had left, worn smooth from overuse, still coming out of him long after there was anyone left to receive it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, lyrical short piece in first person about someone reenacting fake deaths and fake weddings with a partner, blending intimacy and threat.
counterfactuals.output:
# Rehearsals

We got good at dying together. That was the first thing we perfected—not love, not trust, but the choreography of collapse. You'd press two fingers to my throat and find nothing, and I'd let my eyes go soft and unfocused like a window painted over, and we'd hold that tableau until one of us laughed and ruined it.

Practice, you called it. For what, neither of us said.

Tuesday was a wedding. We didn't have rings so we used the pull-tabs from cheap beer, bent into circles that pinched. You wore my only white shirt, sleeves rolled to hide the fraying, and I recited vows I'd stolen from a film neither of us had actually watched to the end. *I take you*, I said, *in sickness and in the long silence after.* You laughed, but your eyes didn't, and I understood that some part of you believed it, the way children believe in games they've invented—fiercely, and only until they don't.

Wednesday I died in the bathtub, fully clothed, water gone cold around me. You found me there and didn't scream. You just knelt on the tile and held my wrist like you were checking for something you already knew wasn't there, and your thumb moved in small circles against my pulse, which was very much alive, thank you, very much *here*—and I wondered if you were disappointed.

We never talked about why. Why the vows, why the rehearsed grief, why we kept trading which one of us got to be the corpse and which one got to grieve beautifully, performatively, with our whole starving chests. Maybe it was that love felt too plain without a blade folded into it somewhere. Maybe we needed to practice losing each other so the real thing, whenever it came, wouldn't be a surprise—just another Tuesday, another Wednesday, a script we'd already memorized.

Thursday you asked me to marry you for real. I said yes and meant it the way I meant the fake ones, which is to say completely, which is to say I don't know how to say yes any other way anymore.

That night I lay very still and let you check for my pulse, and this time when you found it, you didn't smile with relief.

You looked almost sorry.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental flash fiction piece where the narrator's gestures of violence (finger guns, throat slits) become a metaphor for the end of a marriage, ending with an image of a chalk outline.
counterfactuals.output:
# Finger Guns

I do it at breakfast now, the finger gun, thumb cocked back, aimed across the cereal bowls at Marion's temple. *Pow.* She doesn't look up from the paper. This is our language now, the one we invented sometime after the fifteenth year, when regular words started costing too much.

She does the throat slit back at me. One clean drag of her nail, ear to ear, tongue clicking against her teeth for sound effects. It means *you're dead to me* or it means *pass the milk* — we've stopped distinguishing.

The kids don't notice anymore. They've grown up inside this pantomime, this small violence we do instead of the bigger one, the one where somebody says *I don't* and *anymore* in the same sentence. Finger guns are cheaper than lawyers. Throat slits don't require you to divide the record collection.

At night I lie next to her and make the shape with my hand in the dark, pointed at the ceiling, at God maybe, or just at the water stain that's been spreading since March like something growing under the paint. *Pow.* Silent. She's asleep or pretending, which in this house amounts to the same tense.

Sometimes I catch myself doing it at strangers. The mailman. My own face in the bathroom mirror, thumb up, fingers curled, the barrel of my hand pressed to the reflection's forehead. I don't pull the trigger. I just hold it there, this rehearsal, this small mercy of not-yet.

Marion tells our daughter it's a game. Games have rules, though, and ours only has one: nobody actually falls down.

Until the morning I come downstairs and she's lying on the kitchen floor, arms flung wide, tongue out, playing dead so completely that for one white second I believe it, my heart lurching like a dropped plate — and she opens one eye and laughs, and I don't.

I go get the chalk from the driveway, the sidewalk-chalk the kids abandoned last summer, pink and yellow and blue, and I kneel down next to her on the linoleum while she's still laughing, still saying *it's just a joke, come on,* and I trace her outline anyway, slow, careful, the way you'd trace something you wanted to remember the shape of.

When she gets up, the outline stays. A body-shaped hole in the kitchen floor, chalk-white, already exactly the size of everything we're not saying.

She looks down at it a long time.

Then she steps outside the lines, into her slippers, into the rest of the morning, and neither of us cleans it up.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic monologue exploring toxic love through imagery of pretend suicide, pretend gunshots, and pretend wedding rings, with a haunting, ambiguous ending.
counterfactuals.output:
# What We Played At

We used to play at dying, didn't we?
You'd press your fingers to my temple like a barrel,
whisper *bang* soft as a lullaby,
and I'd fall backward into our unmade bed
laughing like it was the funniest thing—
this small rehearsal of an ending.

I didn't know then that love could be
a loaded metaphor,
that every game contains
the shape of what it's imitating.

You gave me a ring made of foil once,
twisted it from a gum wrapper
while we sat on the fire escape,
promised me forever
in a voice that already knew
forever wasn't a place you stayed.

*Till death do us part*, you said,
and we both laughed
because death was just a word then,
just a game we played
with our hands shaped like guns,
with vows shaped like smoke,
with rings that would tarnish
before the metaphor could rust.

I kept pretending to fall.
You kept pretending to shoot.
We kept pretending the wedding
was something other than rehearsal
for all the ways
we'd learn to disappear
from each other
in slow motion.

Somewhere in the pretending
the trigger got real
and the ring got heavier
and I stopped being sure
which one of us was still playing.

Was I ever standing?
Did you ever mean the *forever*?
Or were we always just
two children in a room
practicing our vanishing—

and I'm still there, I think.
Still falling.
Still waiting for you to say
*it was only a game.*

Still waiting for the bang
that tells me
I can stop pretending
to be alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
